title: Joshua 11:16–23
context: The narrator summarizes the conquest from the far south to Mount Hermon in the north. Joshua made war a long time, and no city made peace except Gibeon (Joshua 9). Verse 20 explains that the LORD hardened the hearts of these kings to come against Israel, so that they would be devoted to destruction as he had commanded Moses. This raises a real theological question about divine hardening and human responsibility, which the notes and a key contrast address. Joshua also cuts off the Anakim, the giants who had frightened the spies (Numbers 13:33), leaving a remnant only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. The section ends with the land at rest from war. Yet Joshua 13:1 says much land remained to be possessed, and Judges 1 shows ongoing struggle. Both traditions recognize the summary as true of the decisive campaign, while the work of possession continued. They take both statements seriously rather than forcing them together. As in 11:1–15, both deny that the herem passages license violence today.

verses.text: So Joshua captured all that land, the hill country, all the South, all the land of Goshen, the lowland, the Arabah, the hill country of Israel, and the lowland of the same,
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua captures all the land: the hill country, the South, Goshen, the lowland, the Arabah, and the hill country of Israel with its lowland. The summary is sweeping.

Arminian readers note that the summary celebrates God’s faithfulness, while later chapters show the ongoing responsibility to possess the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the language is comprehensive, emphasizing that God has kept his promise. This Goshen is a region in southern Canaan, not the Goshen in Egypt.

Both traditions read the summary as a true account of the decisive conquest, while recognizing that possession was not yet complete.

verses.text: from Mount Halak, that goes up to Seir, even to Baal Gad in the valley of Lebanon under Mount Hermon. He took all their kings, struck them, and put them to death.
verses.arminianNotes:
From Mount Halak toward Seir to Baal Gad under Mount Hermon, Joshua takes and kills all their kings. The land is described from south to north.

Arminian readers note that the defeat of the kings ended organized resistance, opening the way for Israel to settle.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God delivers the rulers of the land into Israel’s hand, fulfilling his word. The exact locations of Mount Halak and Baal Gad are uncertain.

Both traditions treat the geography cautiously and focus on the fulfillment of God’s promise from one end of the land to the other.

verses.text: Joshua made war a long time with all those kings.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua made war a long time with all those kings. The conquest was not quick.

Arminian readers note that faithfulness requires perseverance; God’s promises are often fulfilled through sustained effort over time. Many infer from Caleb’s age in Joshua 14:7–10 that the campaigns lasted several years.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s timing governed the pace of conquest (compare Exodus 23:29–30, where God says he will drive out the nations little by little).

Both traditions hold the length of the war cautiously and draw from the verse a lesson of patient faithfulness.

verses.text: There was not a city that made peace with the children of Israel, except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took all in battle.
verses.arminianNotes:
No city made peace with Israel except the Hivites of Gibeon; all others were taken in battle. Gibeon is the exception.

Arminian readers note that Gibeon’s choice to seek peace, though made through deception (Joshua 9), shows that a different response was possible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Gibeon’s preservation was God’s providence working through a flawed human act. The rest resisted.

Both traditions see in Gibeon, like Rahab, evidence that Canaanites who turned toward Israel’s God could be spared, a point that bears on how the herem passages are read.

verses.text: For it was of the LORD to harden their hearts, to come against Israel in battle, that he might utterly destroy them, that they might have no favor, but that he might destroy them, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verses.arminianNotes:
It was of the LORD to harden their hearts to come against Israel in battle, so that they would be devoted to destruction, as the LORD commanded Moses. This verse explains the kings’ resistance.

Classical Arminians read the hardening as judicial, God giving over kings already set against him, after centuries of patience (Genesis 15:16). They point to Rahab and Gibeon as evidence that repentance remained possible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God sovereignly ordaining the kings’ resistance as the means of his judgment, as with Pharaoh and Sihon (Deuteronomy 2:30), while holding that the kings acted willingly and God is not the author of sin.

Both traditions affirm God’s rule and human accountability together.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions affirm that the LORD is sovereign over the nations, that the Canaanite kings were responsible for their opposition, and that God is just and not the author of sin. Classical Arminians typically read this hardening as judicial: God confirmed and gave over kings already set against him and his people, after long patience (compare Genesis 15:16), and he did not decree their unbelief in advance. Rahab’s faith in Joshua 2 shows to them that Canaanites could turn to the LORD. Reformed readers typically see God sovereignly ordaining the kings’ resistance as the means of the judgment he had decreed, working through their own willing choices. They link the verse with texts such as Deuteronomy 2:30 and Romans 9:17–18, while holding that the kings acted freely and God is not the author of their sin. The difference concerns how God’s purpose relates to human choice, not whether God rules or people are accountable.

verses.text: Joshua came at that time, and cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah, and from all the hill country of Israel. Joshua utterly destroyed them with their cities.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua cuts off the Anakim from the hill country, Hebron, Debir, Anab, and the hill country of Judah and Israel, destroying them with their cities. The giants feared by the spies are defeated.

Arminian readers note the reversal: the people whose size caused Israel’s unbelief (Numbers 13:33) are defeated by a faithful generation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God overcomes what his people feared most. Joshua 15:13–17 describes Caleb and Othniel taking Hebron and Debir, which interpreters harmonize as a summary here and a detailed account there.

Both traditions draw encouragement that God defeats the giants that frighten his people.

verses.text: There were none of the Anakim left in the land of the children of Israel. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod, did some remain.
verses.arminianNotes:
No Anakim remained in Israel’s land except in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. A remnant survived.

Arminian readers note that the remnant left in these cities would later trouble Israel; incomplete conquest had lasting consequences.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Gath is later named as the home of Goliath (1 Samuel 17:4), and many readers connect him with this surviving remnant, though the text does not say so directly.

Both traditions hold the connection cautiously and see in the remnant a hint that the conquest was not yet complete.

verses.text: So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD spoke to Moses; and Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their divisions by their tribes. Then the land had rest from war.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua took the whole land as the LORD told Moses and gave it to the tribes as an inheritance, and the land had rest from war. Yet Joshua 13:1 says much land remained to be possessed.

Arminian readers note the tension and read the summary as true of the decisive campaign, while the full possession still depended on Israel’s continued faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the tension and read the rest as real but provisional. Hebrews 4:8 teaches that Joshua did not give the final rest, which remains for God’s people.

Both traditions honor both statements rather than forcing them together.
